graft.title: A bench check's value is the last number in divan's output, not a time
graft.need: `tend code checks --run` records each bench check with a value that isn't a measurement. In sylva: bench `structures` (`cargo bench --bench structures`) recorded 240.000, which is the allocation size on the output's last line (`grow: ... 240 B`); bench `forest` (`cargo bench --bench forest`) recorded 102400.000, the iters column of the last row (reorder_children_forest at 100000: `11.82 ns │ 16.02 ns │ 11.91 ns │ 12.01 ns │ 100 │ 102400`). So it seems to take the last number printed. With divan's table, a value per benchmark row (name and args, with its median and unit) is what a bench result means; or, if a check holds one number, a way to name which row and column it is (for example `unit: "flat_rebuild/100000 median"`), so gates (`< 2`, `>= 90`) and trends compare like with like.
graft.use_case: sylva's benches/forest.rs carries the Forest node's speed rule ("at least as fast as a hand-written arena ... checked by benchmarks") and its decisions quote medians (Flat rebuild 338-343 us at 100k). With real values, impl_score's report can show benchmark trends per row, and a gate can hold the rule (forest preorder at or under the arena's) instead of a number that's an iteration count.

answer.text: Built in tend de5a201 (in the next build deployed): when a bench's output is divan's table, the check takes the median of the row its name names, in that row's unit: name a check by its row (`flat_rebuild/100000`, `reorder_children_forest/100000`, or a unique end of a row's path) with the same `cargo bench --bench forest` command, one check per row a gate or trend needs. A check named after the bench itself (`forest`, `structures`) names no row: it records its seconds, as a command printing no number does, rather than a number that's an iteration count. Rows are read by the header's column positions. Tested on the table your ask quoted; not run on sylva's own benches.
